title: Dillon Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Dillon wells have a 71 ft median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and typical completed costs of $10,600-$19,100.
h1: What Dillon, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Within 5 miles of Dillon, Colorado, DWR records show 2,115 permitted wells, including 1,201 recorded as constructed. The local numbers point to relatively shallow wells overall, but mountain bedrock still makes individual results unpredictable.

The median reported depth is 71 feet, and the median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute. Those figures are useful for comparing nearby properties, but they do not guarantee the result on a specific lot. Before buying or building, review neighboring well permits, construction reports, water levels, and the legal use allowed by the permit.

sections.heading: Dillon well depths vary with the mountain ground
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Dillon is 71 feet. The middle half of wells runs from 41 to 153 feet, while the 90th percentile reaches 240 feet. Sixty-two percent are under 100 feet, 32% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 6% are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest record is 845 feet.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer: 2,007 wells do so. That matters when a driller prices a new hole. Granite and gneiss can produce water through fractures, so two nearby lots can require different depths. A bid based only on the 71-foot median may not cover a deeper hole, casing, grout, pump, or difficult access.

sections.heading: A 10 gpm median is a useful starting point
sections.html:
Of the permitted wells that report pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 7.0 and 15.0 gpm. Sixty-one percent report yields from 5 to 15 gpm, and 28% report more than 15 gpm. Eleven percent fall between 1 and 5 gpm. No reported wells are under 1 gpm.

For a buyer, that distribution is encouraging but not a promise of household performance. A well test should show recovery and sustained production, not just a brief pump reading. Confirm the permit's allowed use as well: 62% of the records are domestic or household wells, while monitoring wells make up 21%.

sections.heading: Dillon water levels do not show a simple steady decline
sections.html:
The median static water level is 27 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 14 to 51 feet. That is the water level when the well is not being pumped, not the depth of the well itself. Pump sizing and pressure-tank planning should use the actual well report rather than the area median.

Measurements by decade vary: 15 feet in the 1970s, 49 feet in the 1980s, 31 feet in the 1990s, 55 feet in the 2000s, 34 feet in the 2010s, and 16 feet in the 2020s. This series moves up and down rather than showing a consistent dropping trend. The number of water-level records is limited to 152, so a nearby well's current measurement deserves more weight.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long activity around Dillon
sections.html:
Dillon-area permit records extend from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. Issuance was highest in the 1990s, with 405 permits, followed by 360 in the 2000s. The record includes 236 permits in the 1980s, 224 in the 1970s, 168 in the 2010s, 163 in the 2020s, 148 in the 1960s, and 8 in the 1950s.

The most active drillers in these records are Buena Vista Drilling, with 297 wells; Authorized, with 215; and Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, with 212. These names describe historical permit records, not a recommendation. Ask for current licensing, insurance, references, and a written scope before hiring anyone.

sections.heading: Dillon drilling costs rise quickly in fractured bedrock
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. At the 71-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $4,600 to $7,100. That is not the finished water system.

Adding a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical brings the modeled completed-well range to about $10,600 to $19,100 at the median depth. A lot needing a deeper hole, difficult equipment access, more casing or grout, or additional site work can exceed that range. Get the drilling rate and included equipment in writing, and ask how the price changes if the first hole produces too little water.

sections.heading: Check water quality, dry-hole risk, and the building plan
sections.html:
Environmental records deserve a site-specific review. Within about 10 miles are 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 352 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those records do not prove contamination on a particular parcel, but they are reasons to test existing water and understand nearby land uses, mine workings, and drainage.

Low yield and dry holes remain practical risks in fractured rock, even where nearby wells perform well. Before construction, confirm well location, septic setbacks, access for a drill rig, and the legal water use. An exempt household-use well has limits, including the 35 gpm pumping limit, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin. Check with Colorado DWR before relying on a permit for a new home.

sections.heading: Use nearby records before buying a Dillon lot
sections.html:
Start with wells closest to the parcel, then compare properties in Silverthorne, 3 miles away, and Frisco, 4 miles away, only as broader context. Keystone is 7 miles away, Breckenridge 9 miles, Montezuma 10 miles, and Blue River 12 miles. Ground conditions can change over short distances, so the nearest completed wells matter most.

For an existing home, request the permit, construction report, pump test, static water level, and recent laboratory results. For vacant land, have a driller review access, expected depth, casing and grout requirements, septic placement, and the cost if production is poor. Treat the area medians as planning tools, not guarantees. A well and septic feasibility review before closing can prevent a difficult building decision later.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Dillon, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Dillon is 71 feet. The middle half runs from 41 to 153 feet. Most are under 100 feet, but 32% are between 100 and 300 feet, 6% are between 300 and 600 feet, and the deepest record is 845 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make individual depths unpredictable.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Dillon?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock. At the 71-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $4,600 to $7,100. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $10,600 to $19,100. A deeper hole or difficult access can increase the total.

faq.q: How much water do Dillon wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 7.0 and 15.0 gpm. Sixty-one percent of reported yields are from 5 to 15 gpm, and 28% exceed 15 gpm. A pump test and recovery information are still important because nearby fractured-rock wells can perform differently.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Dillon, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield. Records within about 10 miles include 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 352 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those records do not establish contamination on your parcel. Test the existing well or new source through a qualified laboratory and investigate nearby mine and cleanup history.

faq.q: Can I build a home on a well near Dillon?
faq.a: A buildable lot needs more than a nearby well record. Confirm the Colorado DWR permit and legal use, then check well production, water quality, septic setbacks, drill-rig access, and electrical and trenching requirements. Domestic or household wells make up 62% of local records. An augmentation plan may be required in an over-appropriated basin, so verify water rights before closing.
